endorsements.quote: Consumers should be taught the importance of understanding whether the AI was trained to produce outputs for particular demographics, whether bias is likely to lead to an error or unfair decision, and when not to use or to overrule AI decisions or diagnoses.
AI literacy may be cultivated from the very beginning of training with incorporation of AI content into healthcare professional curricula.
Consumers should therefore have the necessary understanding to explain AI and machine learning, performance and model outputs, as well as limitations such as bias and inaccuracy.

unlisted_practices: Medical schools should incorporate AI education into healthcare professional curricula, tailored to consumers, translators, and developers.
Medical schools should link AI teaching to evidence-based medicine and critical appraisal training.
Medical schools should implement a spiral curriculum that revisits AI concepts throughout training to improve knowledge retention.
Medical schools should provide optional courses, electives, and project-based opportunities for students who wish to become AI translators and developers.
Medical schools should use clinically contextualized examples, datasets, and case-based learning in AI teaching.
Academia and industry should provide opportunities for AI translators and developers to flourish.
Medical schools should use interprofessional education to teach team-based recognition of data bias and bioethical and liability considerations in AI.
Medical schools should assess AI competence using well-designed formative and summative assessments requiring application of knowledge.
Developers should stress test models using adversarial attacks and out-of-distribution testing to identify failure points before deployment.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/educational framework paper proposing an AI curriculum for healthcare professionals based on evidence-based medicine principles.
